newsitem.title: ROMANIA: East Europeans say NATO expansion should go on.
newsitem.headline: East Europeans say NATO expansion should go on.

text.p: East European leaders want NATO's summit in Madrid to give a clear signal that the alliance's first eastward expansion will not be its last.
The democracies which emerged across the region after the 1989 fall of Communism hope that the Madrid summit will usher in a new era, removing post-World War Two divisions of Europe.

"At last ends...the imposed division of our continent. For Poland and for Europe, for us all, this means peace, security, good cooperation," Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski told fellow countrymen last month.

Countries like Poland, which the West left behind the Iron Curtain 50 years ago, say that NATO's first admission of former Cold War enemies should not build new walls between newcomers and those passed over for quick membership.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- the United States' choices for initial alliance expansion -- lead a field of a dozen aspirants seeking to join NATO's security umbrella.

Those three, who enjoy consensus among NATO's 16 members, are certain to be invited to start accession talks when alliance leaders gather in Madrid on Tuesday and Wednesday, although some European allies want Romania and Slovenia included as well.
All three favourites insist that the alliance should not shut its door to other aspirants from Europe's northern and southern rims.
The prospect of gaining NATO membership has encouraged countries across the region to settle chronic disputes with neighbours which had been buried during the Communist era.
Hungary signed a treaty with Romania last year intended to turn old rivalries into a friendship modelled on the French-German relationship of the post-World War Two era.
Poland has launched a new partnership with Ukraine, a large former Soviet republic, and Romania, whose army is the second largest after Poland's among ex-Warsaw Pact members.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu said the new partnership between Warsaw, Kiev and Bucharest might "emerge as a stable and important market in Central Europe".

Constantinescu, whose reformists ended a seven-year leftist grip on power in parliamentary and presidential elections last year, has thanked Romania's traditional friend France for leading European support for the Romanian bid.

"Romania no longer has protectors, now it has powerful friends and allies," he said earlier this month in a reference to prospects for freedom and democracy in the post-communist era, after centuries of Turkish and Russian domination.

Slovenia, which avoided the bloodbath caused by the 1991-92 breakup of old Yugoslavia, has lobbied hard for first-wave admission, saying its membership, like Romania's, would strengthen NATO's southern flank in the volatile Balkans.
Italy has led the European chorus supporting Slovenia's bid. The former Yugoslav republic, on the Adriatic coast, could offer a corridor linking landlocked Hungary to Italy.
Hungary also wants NATO leaders to set a time frame for a further enlargement. Some of the countries rejected this time around say that should happen no later than 1999 or 2000.
"I would find it good if the Madrid summit would name those that could join in the second wave, maybe even giving a time frame," Hungary's foreign minister said last week.

Czech President Vaclav Havel has urged NATO not to rule out future admission for the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, once part of the now-defunct Soviet empire and whose NATO aspirations raise Moscow's hackles.
"Personally I think this wave should not be the last one. On the contrary, it should be the start of the enlargement process," Havel said during a visit to Kiev last Wednesday.

"If republics which emerged from the former Soviet Union, for example the Baltic states, feel they must be in the Euro-Atlantic system represented by NATO, they are fully within their rights to apply for membership and be accepted."
